questions.q: Identify the sentence type of Mrs Fitzgerald's line: "Put your foot down, once an' for all, an' be the mistress of your own house an' the boss of your own family."
questions.a: Imperative sentence (command). A wrong answer (e.g., "declarative" or "interrogative") reveals the student cannot distinguish sentence functions, missing how Fitzgerald's grammatical directness establishes her dominance immediately.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Mrs Pearson's shift from "I can't" to "I won't" after the body-swap matters for the play's theme.
questions.a: "Can't" expresses inability (external constraint); "won't" expresses volitional refusal (agency). The shift grammatically enacts her reclamation of power. A wrong answer treating them as synonyms shows the student misses how modality encodes the central conflict: submissiveness vs. assertion.

questions.q: In the exchange where Doris says "Mum—you'll have to iron my yellow silk" and Mrs Pearson replies "What d'you think I'm doing—whitewashing the ceiling?", identify the grammatical form of Doris's request and the pragmatic force of Mrs Pearson's response.
questions.a: Doris uses a modal necessity construction ("have to" + infinitive) functioning as a demand. Mrs Pearson responds with a rhetorical question (interrogative form, declarative force) employing sarcasm to reject the presupposition of servitude. A wrong answer labeling both as "questions" or "statements" fails to see how form/function mismatch creates the comedy and conflict.

questions.q: Compare the politeness strategies in Mrs Pearson's pre-swap speech ("I'm so fond of them even if they are so thoughtless... I keep dropping a hint") with her post-swap speech to George ("Well, that ought to be a nice change for you"). Analyze the shift in terms of Brown & Levinson's positive/negative face.
questions.a: Pre-swap: heavy positive politeness (apologizing, hedging, claiming shared values) to protect family's face. Post-swap: bald on-record with negative politeness markers ("ought to") used ironically to threaten George's face. The grammatical shift from mitigators ("even if," "suppose") to direct evaluation enacts the power inversion. A wrong answer listing only "she becomes rude" misses the systematic pragmatic recalibration.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the play's resolution—Mrs Pearson reverting to her original personality but with a "firm hand" recommended by Mrs Fitzgerald—is linguistically plausible given the grammatical patterns established. Justify with textual evidence.
questions.a: Plausible because the final stage direction shows her using imperatives ("Seeing that you don't want to go out, I tell you what I thought we'd do") and the family responds with compliance ("No, Mother — whatever you say"). The grammar demonstrates internalized authority: she no longer needs the Fitzgerald persona because the syntactic patterns of command have been normalized. A wrong answer claiming "she goes back to being weak" ignores the textual evidence of sustained imperative mood in the closing scene.

questions.q: Write a 4-line dialogue snippet where Mrs Pearson (post-play) uses a single grammatical structure repeatedly to assert a new boundary with Cyril, without raising her voice. Annotate the structure you chose and why it works.
questions.a: Example: "Cyril, you will put your clothes in the hamper. You will rinse your dishes. You will ask before borrowing. You will remember this routine." Structure: "You will + bare infinitive" (future-as-command). Works because it avoids the negotiability of "please" or "could you" while maintaining calm declarative tone—grammatical firmness without aggression. A poor answer uses mixed structures ("Please do this," "Don't do that") showing lack of control over the chosen grammatical tool.
